ASRS:1850830.s: The flight crew and flight attendants experienced a persistent odor, metallic taste, and burning eyes throughout the flight, which intensified during descent. Maintenance identified the cause as engine oil in the air conditioning packs upon arrival at the gate.

ASRS:1850833.n: ZZZZZ 1B arrival into ZZZZZ. Received clearance 'descent to FL250 at ZZZZZ.' Complied. After ZZZZZ, received clearance 'descend via ZZZZZ 1B, maintain 14 thousand;' We started our VNAV path descend. Passing ZZZZ1, we were given vectors, heading 070 while still descending to 14K. To the northwest of ZZZZ2, we were given clearance 'direct to ZZZZ3 and descent to 10 thousand (or descend and maintain 10 thousand, definitely not DESCEND VIA'). LNAV and VNAVing to ZZZZ3, noticed we are not descending below 14K due to the altitude restrictions in the FMS, and knowing we weren't given descend via for the 10K, I either V/S or LVL CHGed to start descending to 10K. Passing 11.5K, VFR, it seemed odd that they would want us that much lower than published. We asked approach to confirm descend to 10K. ATC responded with we're below the altitude on the arrival, I immediately dialed in something higher in the altitude window and started a climb. At the same time we received CAUTION TERRAIN, ATC came back and said we're given a descend via to 10K and now to climb and maintain 12 thousand. We climbed back up to 12K and completed the arrival and approach. Being a domestic pilot my entire time at [Company], pretty much all of it in ZZZ. This might be the second time I've been to ZZZZ with the previous occasion probably over 6 years ago. Only ever flew into [Country] a handful of times and no [Continent]. I made sure I read all the airport familiarization pages, all the Jepp pages, all the [Country] info in the FOM. And was extremely vigilant regarding 'direct to vs direct' and 'descend via and descend to' clearances. Those were the key words I was listening for. Me and the Captain both agree and the second clearance did not include descend via. I do believe my lack of outside of US experience played a role. I trusted foreign ATC and thought the that low descent was common local procedure. In training and all the distance learning modules, we get hammered on the difference between DIRECT TO and DIRECT. I don't recall as much of an emphasis on DESCEND VIA vs DESCEND UNRESTRICTED (which is official ICAO phraseology on an arrival) and DESCEND TO/DESCEND AND MAINTAIN, which is a FAA phraseology for US arrivals meaning to descend unrestricted. I believe these points should be emphasized in future training modules. In regards to ZZZZ ATC, in my opinion they should only use 2 descent terminologies on arrivals with altitude restrictions. Either DESCEND VIA or DESCEND UNRESTRICTED. Using a DESCEND AND MAINTAIN or DESCEND TO clearance on an arrival with altitude restrictions, from what I can tell is non-standard per our FOM and should not be used. CLEARANCE......Descending Via ZZZZZ 1B except maintain 14,000. Just after ZZZZZ vectored off the STAR to the east for spacing and given a descent to 10,000 ft. with multiple speed changes. Approaching 10,000 ft. in VMC conditions I queried the Controller about our altitude he said we should be at 14,000 ft. descending via. We were on vectors. We immediately initiated a climb to 14,000 ft. and as per his request leveled at 12,000 ft. We were cleared direct to ZZZZ3 and were told to rejoin the STAR. We landed XXL I believe there was a freq change to a new controller who forgot about us. He made no mention of our altitude until I asked him to confirm. There was also no mention of rejoining the STAR.Remain on the STAR/SID to the max extent possible.
ASRS:1850833.s: A crew flying a ZZZZZ 1B arrival descended to 10,000 feet after receiving a "descend to" clearance instead of "descend via," triggering a terrain caution. The pilot climbed to 12,000 feet after ATC clarified the error, attributing the incident to ambiguous phraseology and lack of international experience.

ASRS:1850878.n: During climb thru 1,400 MSL, number 1 engine, left engine, flame out. After confirming left engine had failed, left Engine Stop and Feather was pulled, left prop went to feather. ZZZ Approach was notified of the situation, requested priority handling, I entered on a left downwind for Runway XX, followed QRH procedures and landed without any further issues.Identification - Left engine power lost, left propeller was showing NTS, right rudder pressure was needed to maintain heading.Cause - Left engine component cause it to failed.
ASRS:1850878.s: During climb through 1,400 MSL, the left engine flamed out due to a component failure, requiring feathering and right rudder pressure. The pilot notified ZZZ Approach, executed a left downwind for Runway XX, and landed safely following QRH procedures.

ASRS:1850905.n: On descent into ZZZ a very strong odor consumed the cabin. The smell was sweet and pungent at the same time. The odor was so strong it made my eyes burn, breathing was difficult, I got a headache and it left a metallic taste in my mouth along with mild dizziness. The number 2 and 4 had the same reactions. As we were descending into ZZZ the Flight Attendant 2 (FA2) and myself smelled a strange odor and it got much stronger as we were getting closer to landing. I called to FA1 and he said he smelled the same thing. FA1 said he would inform the Captain. The FA2 and I wet paper towels and placed them over our nose and mouth. After landing the smell went away a little. When we arrived at the gate the mechanics met the aircraft and stated he smelled the odor as soon as we opened the door.
ASRS:1850905.s: Cabin crew reported a strong, sweet, and pungent odor during descent into ZZZ that caused physical symptoms and required wet paper towels for protection. Mechanics confirmed smelling the odor immediately upon opening the aircraft door at the gate.

ASRS:1850924.n: Please repair the flashing FAA beacon on the peak of Mount San Miguel. A non-flashing orange light located below the highest point on the mountain has been substituting for the official FAA beacon. The current light may be emitting from one of the private television or radio antennas/antennae also on the top of the mountain. The flashing beacon is especially important when there is low visibility at night. The abrupt 2,200+ feet elevation change above sea level should have an official FAA beacon to warn the pilots. It is the tallest mountain within 15 miles of the San Diego International Airport. Please also note that this not only is a concern for aircraft, but it may also be a trespassing problem related to the ground access to the top of the mountain.
ASRS:1850924.s: A pilot reported that the FAA beacon on Mount San Miguel is flashing incorrectly, with a non-flashing orange light from a private antenna substituting for it. The reporter stated this creates a hazard for aircraft near San Diego International Airport, especially during low visibility at night.

ASRS:1850939.n: I was doing a flight with my private student and was in the traffic pattern for Runway XXL at ZZZ, on the third lap in the pattern I saw something in my peripheral vision. My student couldn't see it due to the altitude the engine cowling was blocking his vision, there was a drone that was at approximately 1,100 ft. I quickly pulled the yoke back to gain altitude to avoid the drone that was right in front of us. I reported it to the ZZZ Tower and they asked me questions about what happened, the drone activity was not a part of the ZZZ ATIS, and the Controllers did not see it. When I landed the plane I had to call the ZZZ Tower and give them a little more details and filed a safety report with my flight school.
ASRS:1850939.s: A flight instructor and student in a private aircraft encountered a drone at 1,100 ft while in the traffic pattern for Runway XXL at ZZZ. The instructor executed an avoidance maneuver to gain altitude, as the drone was not listed on the ATIS and was unseen by controllers.
